blocks.text: Stacks exist because one situation shows up again and again in computing: **the most recent unfinished thing has to be finished first**. A function that called another function can't continue until that call returns. An editor's undo must reverse your **latest** change before older ones. A closing bracket must match the **latest** opening bracket. Whenever "latest first" is the rule, a stack is the natural tool.
1. The call stack: how every program runs

Every time a function is called, your computer pushes a **frame** onto the **call stack**: the function's local variables and the place to come back to when it finishes. When the function returns, its frame is popped and the caller carries on exactly where it paused. Recursion is nothing more than this stack growing and shrinking:

blocks.alt: The call stack while computing factorial(3). main is at the bottom, then factorial(3), factorial(2) and factorial(1) on top. Each call pushes a frame; each return pops one. factorial(1) returns 1, factorial(2) returns 2, factorial(3) returns 6.
blocks.caption: The function called last is the first to finish.
Watch the frames pile up on the way down and come off in reverse on the way back.

blocks.text: If the base case is missing, frames keep piling up until the call stack runs out of space and the program crashes with a **stack overflow**. And because recursion is a stack, any recursive algorithm can be rewritten with an explicit stack of your own — you'll do exactly that in **Decode String**.

Text editors keep every change on an **undo stack**. Undo pops the latest change and reverses it — then pushes it onto a **redo stack**, so redo can put it back. Making a brand-new change clears the redo stack, because the old future no longer makes sense.

blocks.alt: Two stacks side by side. The undo stack holds the changes typed 'Hi', made bold and added '!', with add '!' on top. After pressing undo once, add '!' moves from the top of the undo stack to the redo stack.

blocks.text: Your browser's **back** and **forward** buttons work the same way: every page you leave is pushed on the back stack; pressing back pops it and pushes the current page onto the forward stack.

Code editors highlight matching brackets, and compilers reject `(a + b]`. Both use a stack: every opening bracket is pushed, and every closing bracket must match the one on top — the **most recently opened** bracket that is still open.

blocks.alt: The text { [ ( ) ] } with arcs connecting each pair: ( with ), [ with ], { with }. The innermost pair closes first, so the last bracket opened is the first one closed.

blocks.text: **Valid Parentheses**, later in this course, is this exact check.
Push every item, then pop them all: they come out **backwards**. It's the simplest way to reverse a word, a list of steps, or the path back out of a maze.
5. Backtracking: finding your way out of a maze

Exploring a maze, you choose a path at every junction. When you hit a dead end, you go back to the **most recent** junction that still has an unexplored path. Keeping the junctions on a stack does exactly that — this is **depth-first search**, the engine behind solving mazes, Sudoku and many graph problems.

blocks.alt: A maze path from Start through junctions A, B and C. C leads to a dead end, so the explorer pops C and returns to B, the most recent junction with an untried path. The stack holds Start, A, B, C with C on top.

blocks.text: Why not just use an array?
A stack usually is an array underneath — so why talk about stacks at all? Because the restriction is the point:

items: **It states your intent.** Code that only pushes and pops tells the reader "latest first" without a comment.
**It prevents bugs.** If nothing can touch the middle, nothing can corrupt it by accident.
**It guarantees speed.** Every operation is O(1); there is no slow operation to call by mistake.
**It's a thinking tool.** Once you see "latest unfinished thing first", the algorithm often writes itself.
Stacks model **"the most recent unfinished thing first"**.
Every program runs on a **call stack**; recursion is that stack growing and shrinking.
Undo/redo and back/forward are **two stacks** passing items between them.
Bracket matching, reversing and backtracking (DFS) are all stack algorithms.
A stack is an array with a **promise**: only the top is ever touched.
